newsitem.title: FRANCE: Belgrade opposition chief warns against sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade opposition chief warns against sanctions.

text.p: Vesna Pesic, a leader of Belgrade's opposition movement, cautioned Washington and Europe on Tuesday against freezing trade deals with Serbia and urged them to target President Slobodan Milosevic personally.

Pesic, in Paris at the invitation of opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, said a decision by electoral officials on Tuesday to award victory to the opposition in the Belgrade city council would signal a turnaround if confirmed.
"I remain cautious because there are 48 hours during which appeals against the decision can be made," Pesic, who met French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette on Monday, told a news conference.
"If the results are recognised then yes, it would be a turnaround because up to now the government has always said that elections would not be recognised," she said.

Electoral officials in Belgrade overruled a district court and awarded victory to the opposition Zajedno coalition in the capital's assembly. Independent media said a court in the second city of Nis had made a similar ruling there.

Asked whether the United States and European Union countries should break off trade relations with Belgrade to back the opposition movement, Pesic answered: "In general, economic sanctions or isolation as of the Yugoslav republic in the past are not good.
"The people are the first to feel the consequences. Personalised pressure, targeted much more on Milosevic, would be much more efficient than sanctions.

"The international community could publicly declare that he is not eligible," she said, without elaborating. She added that he "should be asked a series of questions about his role in the war" in former Yugoslavia.

Jospin praised the "strength, genuineness, courage and perseverance of the democracy movement" which aims to force the Socialist government to reinstate November municipal election results in 14 cities.

The election moves came just hours after some half a million people braved freezing temperatures to jam Belgrade for an Orthodox New Year's Eve protest that was the biggest yet mounted against Milosevic.
